about: CIHR Postdoctoral Fellow | Brown Lab, University of Victoria Former Instructor in Neuroscience at Weill Cornell Medicine & Burke Neurological Institute. Member of the Ratan Lab (Laboratory for Neural Redox Biology and Homeostatic Transcription). I am interested in how physical forces shape cellular and axonal fate in stroke pathophysiology. When a stroke occurs, secondary mechanical stressors like hematoma expansion, intracranial pressure, and tissue edema fundamentally alter the physical environment of the brain. Concurrently, dysregulation of brain iron and ion homeostasis severely compromises metabolic stability. My work explores how these biomechanical and biochemical cues are transduced into cellular redox signals, and how this crosstalk fuels either axonal degeneration and vulnerability to cell death, or conversely, plasticity and resilience. Above all, my priorities are translational rigour and designing basic neuroscience for clinical relevance.

headline: Important findings from a collaborative #UCalgary research study led by Dr. Tuan Trang , PhD, show a deeper understanding of communication in the body during opioid withdrawal. Co-led by researchers Drs. Charlie Kwok, PhD, Erika Harding, PhD, and Nicole Burma, MD’21, PhD’21, the study was recently published in the journal Nature Communications. Dr. Trang’s lab has been studying how opioids affect key pain centres in the nervous system, and in 2017, the research team made a breakthrough discovery – that probenecid effectively reduces opioid withdrawal in rodents. Recently they unraveled how the medication disrupts the abnormal brain-spinal cord communication that occurs during opioid withdrawal. “I don’t think I’ve had a day in clinic in the last five years where I haven’t had a patient tell me they want to reduce the opioids they are taking,” says pain clinician and clinical lead Dr. Lori Montgomery , MD’03. “The problem is there are limited options to support them, and the withdrawal symptoms can be crippling.” Drs. Montgomery and Trang are now recruiting for a clinical trial to test probenecid, which is a safe, well tolerated drug for gout, as a potential treatment for disabling withdrawal symptoms. headline: Men’s Mental Health | Helping Men & Teams Perform Under Pressure | Family Therapist & Speaker
connections: I’m starting to wonder if we’ve been asking the wrong question. For years, we’ve asked: “Why won’t men talk about their mental health?” But over the last few months, I’ve had the opportunity to sit with men in therapy offices, at Shed Talk gatherings, over coffee, during shared work, and around tables where the conversation was never supposed to be about mental health. And yet, that’s exactly where it went. Not because anyone pushed. Not because anyone had the perfect intervention. But because there was enough trust and connection for the conversation to unfold naturally. Maybe the challenge isn’t that men don’t want support. Maybe it’s that we’ve underestimated the importance of belonging, shared experience, and the way trust and connection develop. I recently wrote an article exploring this idea, and it’s left me with one question that I can’t seem to let go of: What conditions need to exist before men want to talk? I’d genuinely love to hear your thoughts. What have you noticed?
about: I help people and teams understand how mental health shows up under pressure. That experience shaped how I see mental health. It’s not separate from performance. It’s not something that only shows up in crisis. It’s a system—one that is always influencing how people think, act, communicate, and function. In my clinical work, I support individuals, couples, and families navigating trauma, anxiety, ADHD, and relational challenges. But over time, my focus has expanded beyond the therapy room. I’m particularly interested in how these same patterns show up in teams and organizations—especially in high-pressure environments where people are expected to perform, lead, and make decisions under stress. A lot of what we label as “behavioural issues” are actually predictable responses to pressure, environment, and system dynamics. When we understand that, everything shifts. Communication improves. Conflict makes more sense. People stop seeing themselves—or each other—as the problem. My work integrates trauma-informed care, stress physiology, and systems thinking to help people and teams build capacity, improve communication, and function more effectively under pressure. Whether I’m working with a family, a team, or an organization, the goal is the same: To create environments where people can think more clearly, respond more effectively, and show up at their best, even when things are hard. headline: Operator and Scale Leader | Founder–Operator Mindset | Building and Scaling Health & Service Platforms | Hearing, Cognition, Telehealth
connections: 🔊 Levels of Listening: A Journey for Educators and Social Professionals In teaching, mentoring, and supporting others, listening is more than hearing words—it's a skill we refine over time. Justin Wright outlines five levels of listening that resonate deeply with those of us in education and social professions: 1️⃣ Waiting to Talk (Self-focused) You're quiet, but only because you're preparing your response. 2️⃣ Hearing the Words (Distracted) You catch parts of the conversation, but your attention drifts. 3️⃣ Understanding the Message (Focused) You’re tuned in—not just to the words, but their meaning. You listen to understand, not to reply. 4️⃣ Recognizing Emotions (Empathetic) You sense their emotional state. You hear how they feel, not just what they say. 5️⃣ Hearing What’s Unsaid (Fully Present) You pick up on the deeper meaning—the things they struggle to express and what they need you to hear. 🎓 As educators, we move through these levels—often daily. The best among us learn to dwell in levels 4 and 5, where real connection and transformation happen. 💬 Which level do you find yourself operating in most often? How do you help your students or colleagues develop deeper listening? #EducationLeadership #EmpatheticListening #ProfessionalDevelopment #SocialImpact #TeachingExcellence #ActiveListening

connections: The psoas muscle, the respiratory diaphragm, and the brain form an interconnected physical and neurological feedback loop. Tension in the deep core can restrict breathing and signal stress to the brain, while slow diaphragmatic breathing can calm the nervous system and help release physical holding patterns. The Physical Connection: Psoas and Diaphragm Shared fascia: The psoas and the respiratory diaphragm connect physically through connective tissue ( fascia) and meet at the spine. Movement partners: When you breathe deeply, the moving diaphragm naturally massages and influences the psoas. Restriction: A tight or guarded psoas can restrict full movement of the diaphragm, leading to shallow breathing. The Neurological Connection: The Brain and Stress Fight-or-flight response: The psoas reacts to perceived danger by bracing or tightening, which is controlled by the older, instinctive areas of the brain and central nervous system. The feedback loop: A chronically tight psoas sends ongoing signals of physical threat back to the brain. The brain interprets this tension as stress, keeping the sympathetic nervous system active. Down-regulation: Conscious, slow diaphragmatic breathing stimulates the vagus nerve and signals safety to the brain, helping break the cycle of stress and physical tension. #psoas #brain #neuroscience #skillcourt

connections: Storytelling is an essential part of being human. Stories stimulate the 🧠 and change the way we act in our lives. When we engage with a narrative, our brains simulate the events, creating vivid mental images and emotional responses, which can lead to increased memory retention and a greater understanding of the story's message. Here's some examples of how storytelling affects the brain: •Increased Empathy and Memory: Stories, especially those with emotional content, can trigger the release of oxytocin, the "bonding hormone," which promotes feelings of empathy and connection with characters and their experiences. This increased empathy can make stories more memorable and relatable. •Enhanced Learning and Retention: Stories help us connect new information to existing knowledge, making it easier to understand and remember. The emotional engagement associated with storytelling signals to the brain that the information is important, leading to deeper storage in memory. •Activation of Multiple Brain Areas: Unlike simply listing facts, storytelling activates various brain regions, including those related to motor cortex, emotion, and visual processing, creating a more immersive and engaging experience. This holistic brain activation contributes to better understanding and recall. •Shifting Perception and Inspiring Action: Stories can reshape our perception of the world and even inspire behavioral changes. By creating emotional connections and demonstrating the consequences of actions, stories can motivate us to learn, empathize, and potentially change our own lives. Overall, telling stories helps us connect to others, make meaning, organize our lives into a coherent narrative and immerse ourselves in others’ tales. While we share stories, we are also improving our mental health and well-being. Learn more: https://lnkd.in/gNtiBYSW One love #brain #storytelling … more

about: I’m an MD/PhD candidate at the University of Alberta, training at the intersection of ophthalmology, medical genetics, and artificial intelligence (AI). My work is driven by a broad but practical goal: to better understand genetic eye disease in ways that improve diagnosis, clarify disease mechanisms, and ultimately support more effective care. My research spans several interconnected areas. I study variants of uncertain significance using computational and molecular biology approaches, investigate the biology of genes and proteins implicated in ocular disease, explore newer sequencing strategies for patients who remain undiagnosed after standard genetic testing, and examine the clinical and biological basis of understudied eye diseases. Across these projects, I am especially interested in linking mechanistic insight with clinical relevance rather than treating them as separate worlds. A parallel thread of my work is focused on AI in medicine. I am interested in how AI can make research, diagnostics, and therapeutics more efficient, accurate, and meaningful for patients. I care just as much about education in this space. I co-founded the AI in Medical Systems Society (AIMSS) and co-designed an AI in Healthcare course that reaches lots of learners across medicine, graduate studies, and the broader public. Since 2025, I have also been delivering AI literacy lectures to health professions learners across multiple stages of training, from nursing and medical school to residency and beyond. Getting this right matters because the gap between what AI can do and what clinicians (and the general public) understand about it has real consequences for patient care. I am training to become an ophthalmologist-scientist-innovator: someone who can move fluidly between clinical problems, biological discovery, technological development, and education. I hope to build a career in which questions that arise at the bedside can be investigated at the bench, shaped by computation and innovation, and translated back into patient care more thoughtfully and more quickly/efficiently.

connections: What do The Beatles have to do with the invention of the CT scanner? At first glance… absolutely nothing. But the story actually runs through EMI, the record company behind the Beatles. In the 1960s, Beatles record sales nearly doubled EMI’s profits, giving the company the resources to fund ambitious research projects. One of those projects was led by engineer Godfrey Hounsfield, who went on to invent computed tomography (CT) and change diagnostic medicine forever. The first clinical CT brain scan took place in 1971, opening a new era of medical imaging. In this short video, we explore: • The strange connection between rock music and medical imaging • How CT reconstruction works • Why radiation safety, ALARA, and dose monitoring matter today • The role of imaging informatics in managing modern imaging systems Sometimes the history of healthcare technology has some very unexpected connections. 🎥 Watch here: https://lnkd.in/gPmyr999 #CTScan #PatientSafety #ALARA #RadiationSafety

about: I am a Ph.D. researcher at GIGA Neuroscience, Faculty of Medicine, University of Liège, specializing in cortical brain organoids as a model system to study cortex maturation and neurodegenerative diseases, particularly Alzheimer’s disease. My research aims to elucidate the molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying cortical development and neurodegeneration, leveraging advanced stem cell technologies and organoid-based models. A key focus of my work is the role of Microtubule-Associated Protein Tau (MAPT) in cortical maturation and Alzheimer’s disease pathogenesis. MAPT plays a crucial role in neuronal differentiation and cytoskeletal stability, and its dysregulation is a hallmark of tauopathies, including Alzheimer's disease. By investigating MAPT dynamics in cortical organoids, I aim to uncover its contributions to neuronal development, synaptic integrity, and neurodegenerative processes, providing insights into both normal brain maturation and disease progression. By integrating cellular neuroscience, molecular biology, and bioengineering approaches, my work seeks to enhance the physiological relevance of cortical organoids, providing novel insights into human brain development and disease pathology. Additionally, I am involved in collaborative efforts to refine organoid-based models for translational applications, with the goal of identifying potential therapeutic targets for neurodegenerative disorders. I welcome collaborations and interdisciplinary discussions on cortical development, brain organoid technology, and neurodegenerative disease modeling.

connections: The Brain-Immune Connection 🧠 (New Findings) The nervous and immune systems were once seen as separate control centers. New work shows this divide doesn’t hold up. Instead, they form a single, integrated network that coordinates responses to stress, circadian rhythms, infection, and tissue injury. Neurons and immune cells share a common signaling language - neurotransmitters, cytokines, and hormones - enabling constant, two-way communication. Neural activity shapes immune cell development and function, while immune signals feed back to influence mood, cognition, and behavior. This interaction can be understood in two ways: 📍 Spatially — communication in the brain, within peripheral organs, and across long distances ⏱️ Temporally — how neural signals guide immune cell development, distribution, and execution of responses Bottom line: the nervous and immune systems don’t just interact—they co-regulate brain–body health, helping explain links between stress, inflammation, and mental health, and opening new paths for therapy. Reference: Leunig A., Gianeselli M., Russo S.J., Swirski F.K. Connection and communication between the nervous and immune systems Nature Reviews Immunology (2025) #Neuroscience #Immunology #Healthcare

connections: I deeply value authenticity and vulnerability, so to put my money where my mouth I am going to be vulnerable and authentic. When I talk about using data to improve people's lives, it is because I do it for myself. These are images from my personal journal; a place where I record my own data, as well as break down my thoughts and feelings. It is time consuming, and I don't often want to keep up with it, but I have found important benefits from doing all this every month. From this practice, I learned that I can fall asleep easier when I drop off some of my thoughts that I carried all day, that it helps me be more accountable and mindful about following through on healthy habits, and it has helped me take a bad day back to an okay day. All of this information that I have kept has allowed me to make connections between my mood and my behaviours. The connections help me recognize where I can improve, when I need to be gentle with myself, and most importantly, when I need to reach out for help. I believe that knowing oneself is the first requirement before anyone can change the world around them. You never know what you'll find when you check in with yourself. #mentalhealth #bulletjournal #authenticity … more

connections: 🧠 Electrical Artifacts An EEG system is designed to detect electrical activity generated by the brain—but it can also detect unwanted electrical signals from the surrounding environment. These unwanted signals are known as electrical artifacts. If they are not recognized, they can obscure cerebral activity, reduce recording quality, and occasionally mimic pathological EEG patterns. Some of the most common electrical artifacts include: ⚡ 50/60 Hz Interference – The classic "mains" artifact caused by alternating current (AC) power lines. It appears as a regular, sinusoidal waveform affecting multiple channels. 🔌 Ground Loops – Occur when multiple grounding paths create circulating electrical currents, introducing unwanted noise into the recording. 🖥️ Electrical Equipment – Nearby monitors, infusion pumps, ventilators, computers, and other medical devices can generate electromagnetic interference that contaminates the EEG. 📱 Mobile Phones & Wireless Devices – Radiofrequency emissions from phones and wireless electronics may produce intermittent high-frequency artifacts, particularly when devices are close to the EEG equipment. ⚠️ Poor Grounding & Inadequate Shielding – Loose ground connections, damaged cables, or insufficient shielding make the EEG system more susceptible to external electrical interference. The good news is that most electrical artifacts are preventable. Simple measures such as maintaining low electrode impedance, ensuring proper grounding, securing cable connections, using shielded cables, and keeping unnecessary electrical devices away from the recording area can dramatically improve EEG quality. 💡 A useful clue: Electrical artifacts often affect many channels simultaneously and do not follow normal neuroanatomical patterns. Before interpreting a suspicious waveform, always ask whether the recording environment—not the patient's brain—is the true source. High-quality EEG interpretation begins with a high-quality recording. Eliminating electrical interference allows genuine cerebral activity to be seen clearly, leading to more accurate diagnoses and better patient care. #EEG #ClinicalNeurophysiology #EEGTechnologist #EEGArtifacts #Electroencephalography #Neurology #Neurophysiology #Epilepsy #MedicalEducation #BrainMonitoring

connections: I believe we are all made of stories. The stories we tell ourselves, and the stories others tell about us. I think these stories have the power to propel us to the tops of mountains or drag us down into the mud. If this sounds a little messy, it’s because it is. Life is messy. Being human is hard, and you don’t have to do it alone. Part of my story, journeying from a 20 year career in arts marketing and communications to therapist, involved falling down a mountain—hard. And then getting back up again a million fucking times. My hiking accident didn’t just leave me with a paralyzed right hand and chronic pain, it has gifted me another kick at that proverbial can... My first career in arts communication was fuelled by stories and community, and I see it now as a bit of a superpower; to listen, to learn, and to be able to hold space for someone else’s story. I couldn’t really know that privilege when I was younger. But now, knee deep in midlife, I am leaning into a new direction. As a genuine and compassionate mental health advocate, I am embracing my lived experiences to help others on their journey. The mountains and nature have long been a personal source of healing, humility, inspiration, and awe for me. I have experience in a variety of backcountry and recreational outdoor pursuits, and I tailored my early graduate course work to exploring ecopsychology; the theoretical and clinical applications of eco therapy, and the biological connections between biophilia and our mental health. After a break in my studies to heal and kick morphine and nerve meds to the curb, I pivoted my capstone research to explore the role resilience and personal narrative play in counselling those living with chronic pain. So when my head isn’t buried in a book or a research study, and my hands aren’t holding a protest sign or caring for someone; my soul will be in the woods, on the water, and up some rock. Onward. Be kind to each other. And go BREATHE in the mountains!

headline: La version française suit 📣 The CAPS|ACPP 2024 National Postdoctoral Survey Report is now available! Drawing on more than a decade of survey data, the report provides an important look at how the postdoctoral experience in Canada is evolving — from compensation and cost of living to career expectations, well-being, and workplace equity. Some of the key findings include: 💰 Compensation & Cost of Living: Median postdoc salaries have increased to $57,500, but rapidly rising living expenses continue to put significant financial pressure on postdoctoral scholars. 🔬 Changing Career Goals: Interest in tenure-track academic careers continues to decline, while more postdocs are considering opportunities in industry, government, NGOs, consulting, and other sectors. 🧠 Wellbeing & Benefits: 86% of postdocs reported experiencing mental health issues, highlighting the urgent need for stronger wellbeing support. Limited access to extended health benefits also continues to create barriers to receiving care. ⚖️ Equity & Workplace Experience: Compared to 2020, more respondents do not plan to stay in or return to Canada, largely driven by temporary foreign workers and citing issues related to limited job opportunities, financial reasons, or personal reasons. The findings reinforce the importance of building a postdoctoral system in Canada that provides fair compensation, better benefits, diverse career development opportunities, and stronger support throughout the postdoctoral experience. 📖 Read the full 2024 National Postdoctoral Survey Report and explore the recommendations here: https://lnkd.in/guqQrhWA #Postdocs #PostdoctoralResearch #CAPSACPP #CanadianResearch #ResearchCommunity #AcademicCareers #HigherEducation #ResearchPolicy -- 📣 Le rapport de l’Enquête nationale 2024 de CAPS|ACPP sur les postdoctorantes et postdoctorants est maintenant disponible! Voici quelques-unes des conclusions majeures : 💰 Rémunération et coût de la vie : Le salaire médian des postdocs s'élève maintenant à 57 500 $. Toutefois, l'augmentation fulgurante du coût de la vie continue d’exercer une pression financière importante sur la communauté postdoctorale. 🔬 Évolution des objectifs de carrière : L’intérêt pour les carrières universitaires menant à la permanence continue de diminuer, tandis qu’un nombre croissant de postdocs envisagent des possibilités de carrière dans l’industrie, le gouvernement, les ONG, le secteur de la consultation et d’autres domaines. 🧠 Bien-être et avantages sociaux : 86 % des postdocs ont déclaré avoir vécu des problèmes de santé mentale, ce qui souligne le besoin urgent de renforcer les mesures de soutien au bien-être. L’accès restreint aux régimes complémentaires d’assurance maladie demeure un obstacle à l’obtention de soins. 🔁 Équité et expérience professionnelle : En comparaison avec l’année 2020, une plus grande part des répondants ne projettent pas de rester au Canada ou d’y revenir. connections: You have 24 hours every day. How you spend them impacts everything. I've seen leaders burn out trying to do everything. And I've watched their teams feel the ripple effects. It’s not about working less. It's about making space for what matters most. That's where the 8-8-8 Rule helps: 8 hours for your personal life. 8 hours for work. 8 hours for sleep. 🧘 For Your Personal Life The leaders who thrive prioritize rest and relationships. You can't pour into others when your own cup is empty. And your team feels it when you’ve stopped looking after yourself. → Set a clear end to workday → Block time for movement and connection → Mute notifications after hours 💼 For Your Work It’s all about how you use your hours throughout the day. Focused, intentional time beats constant availability. And your team needs your clarity more than your clocked-in hours. → Block time for deep work → Schedule essential meetings only → Protect distraction-free focus time 😴 For Your Sleep Sleep isn't a luxury. It's the foundation of every decision. Without it, you're leading on autopilot. And poor sleep quality destroys good judgment. → Keep a consistent bedtime → Wind down without screens → Treat rest as a responsibility But when you give time to all three — yourself, your work, and your rest — You’ll lead with more clarity and presence. That’s the kind of leadership that lasts. ♻️ If this resonates, repost for your network. 📌 Follow Amy Gibson for more leadership insights.

headline: Dementia Advocate | Community Partnerships | Public Speaker | Trainer | Improving lives after a dementia diagnosis
connections: Hi, I'm Kelly Reeves. I am passionate about helping people live well with dementia and challenging the stigma that too often surrounds a diagnosis. My work is grounded in person-centred care and a human rights approach, championing choice, dignity and identity while focusing on people's strengths rather than their limitations. A key part of my practice is the use of music. Drawing on music therapy principles and personalised playlists, I have seen first-hand the power music has to unlock connection, evoke memories and support emotional wellbeing, even for people living with advanced Alzheimer's disease. Alongside my professional work, I share my lived experience as a daughter. My mum was diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease in 2017, and through our journey together I use storytelling, education and social media to show that there is still joy, connection and purpose after a dementia diagnosis. Whether I'm building partnerships, delivering training, speaking to communities or raising awareness online, my mission remains the same: Working together to help people live well with dementia.

She received a B.A. in International Relations from The George Washington University and a Ph.D. in Neuroscience from the University of California, Los Angeles, followed by postdoctoral training in translational neuropsychiatry at the National Institute of Mental Health. Dr. Martinowich’s research focuses on understanding how gene expression programs within defined cell populations and neural circuits contribute to human brain function and neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative disease. Her research program integrates spatially resolved transcriptomics, single-cell genomics, and data-driven computational approaches with experimental models, with an emphasis on postmortem human brain tissue. This work aims to identify molecular and genetic mechanisms underlying disease vulnerability and to validate these findings in human cell-based systems and rodent models.

connections: Dear All I am pleased to share with you this issue, dedicated to the anthropological challenges of neuroscience, which I co-edited with Fabrice Jotterand . It Les Annales des Mines Série Enjeux Numériques. Summary and all articles --> https://lnkd.in/ed7cthfr Les Annales des Mines post --> https://lnkd.in/eNZnp7Xd Exploring #neuroethics as a discipline and the ethical issues surrounding #neuroscience , #neurotechnologies , #AI , and #NeuroAI inevitably leads to philosophical, anthropological, spiritual, and legal reflections. Together with Fabrice Jotterand , we sought to give this issue an international dimension, in both French and English, by bringing together the perspectives of researchers and authors from France, the United States and Chile We also sought to highlight the interconnection between #neuroethics , #bioethics , #neurolaw , and #neurorights , as well as the OECD-OCDE ’s recommendations for 2019 and UNESCO ’s recommendations for 2025. The contributions gathered here thus explore philosophical, anthropological, governance, and clinical perspectives as well as issues related to research whether involving human or non-human subjects and their societal implications. Finally, this issue also offers a space for spiritual reflection through Protestant and Catholic perspectives Indeed, it was difficult to discuss the brain—the seat of consciousness and the person—without addressing what lies at the very heart of our humanity. The goal here is not to align with a particular cause or a specific form of spirituality. Rather, it is to address the unsettling questions raised by interventions on the brain using #neurotechnologies , which are currently booming in contemporary societies, including for non-medical purposes. These questions necessarily call for a plurality of perspectives and disciplines. #Neuroethics #Neuroéthique #bioéthique #bioethics #neurotechnologies #neurotechnology #AI #NeuroAI #neurorights #Neurolaw #cognitive #AIethics #neurosciences

connections: The Paradox of Experience: How Can We Grow If We’re Never Given the Chance? It’s a cycle many graduates know too well. To get a job, you need experience — but to gain experience, you need a job. For so many talented people, this cycle becomes a wall. Recruiters often seek highly skilled candidates with years of experience, but right after graduation, very few companies are willing to offer that first real opportunity. Referrals play a big role in hiring — and while they aren’t bad, they can unintentionally close doors for others. If you live in a city or country where your skills don’t match the local job market, building those connections becomes even harder. You might find yourself applying to companies far away, where you know no one who can refer you. And when months turn into a year or more without real opportunities, burnout hits hard. It’s easy to feel lost, to step away from the career you once loved — not because you stopped believing, but because life’s realities don’t wait. Bills, responsibilities, and survival come first. Still, I believe in persistence. In fighting for your dreams. But we must also remember — not everyone starts from the same place. As professionals, leaders, and recruiters, let’s give more chances to those who are eager to learn and grow. Potential can’t always be measured in years of experience. And to companies — yes, profit matters, but people matter more. Not every new hire will be perfect. Some may struggle. But others could become game-changers — the kind of people who bring new energy, new ideas, and help others grow. Let’s revive what truly makes us human — empathy, opportunity, and belief in each other — instead of constantly chasing the money race. Because sometimes, all someone needs is one opportunity to prove what they’re truly capable of. #JobSearch #CareerGrowth #EarlyCareer #Opportunities #Hiring #Recruitment #TalentAcquisition #FutureOfWork #HiringPractices #HumanFirst #EmpathyAtWork #PeopleOverProfit #Motivation #Resilience

about: I'm a research software developer specializing in medical imaging and open science. I build and maintain open-source scientific software used by medical imaging and neuroimaging labs around the world. I've spent most of my career in MRI physics: first as a researcher, now mostly on the software side. My PhD is in Biomedical Engineering (McGill), and my research has picked up 1,850+ citations to date. I'm the lead maintainer of qMRLab, a quantitative MRI analysis toolbox adopted internationally, and of AxonDeepSeg, a deep learning tool for segmenting axons and myelin in histology images. I also co-authored and edited an interactive online course on quantitative MRI, with live, in-browser code and visualizations. As a personal project, I designed and shipped MR Studio (mrstudio.app), a web app for building publication-quality MRI pulse sequence diagrams. A recurring thread in my work is reproducibility: I led an international reproducibility challenge on T1 mapping with 30+ contributors across multiple sites, co-authored an extension to BIDS — a widely adopted community standard for organizing neuroimaging data — and have contributed to NeuroLibre, a platform for publishing fully reproducible research. I also work on the communication side of science. I was the Deputy Editor for Scientific Outreach at Magnetic Resonance in Medicine — the field's flagship journal — for five years, and lead the digital content team at MRM Highlights, interviewing researchers about new work and making it readable. Day to day, I work mostly in Python and MATLAB, plus git, CI, Docker, and the occasional AWS deployment. I engineer the software around tools like AxonDeepSeg: packaging, testing, releases — everything that makes a research model usable by researchers in other fields. I work in English and French. about: Co-Founder and CEO of Aelo Neurotech. Doing for the brain what Whoop, Garmin and Oura do for the body. Aelo is wearable neurotech for the real world. We use fNIRS (the same class of measurement as an fMRI scanner) to read real-time activity in the prefrontal cortex, your focus and decision centre, through something you'd actually want to wear. That becomes clear, personal metrics led by CoreScore, a forward-looking read on how ready your brain is for what's coming. Measured against your own baseline. You versus you. Our metrics are our product, not the cap. Sport-led first, with defence and high-performance industry alongside. At the start of this year, being a founder and CEO again was honestly the last thing I wanted. Five years building my previous company (wearable neurotech, as it happens) took me to the limits of my resilience, and I needed to find those limits before I could properly recharge. So I got up some mountains, saw a lot of live music, and spent a few happy months on fractional and advisory work. Then the neurotech world drew me back in . . . the pull of building something nobody's done before. If anything, the experience, and the mistakes (mostly the mistakes!), have me more confident, and I'd like to think more capable, than I've ever been. I'm always happy to help other founders. Having been through the wringer of building and raising, I now do a bit of mentoring and advising for early-stage teams on a pro bono basis, particularly purpose-driven startups in health, wellness and anything that genuinely matters. If that's you, say hello. Before all the brain stuff: 25 years in brand, marketing and events. Ops Director at the UK's largest experiential agency, then founder and MD of Jump, a full-service creative agency working with everyone from Burger King and Disney to a country house hotel on the Isle of Mull. Outside work, live music keeps me sane (20+ gigs last year), there's usually vinyl on my dad's old turntable, I run, and I brave Scotland's cold water when I'm feeling brave enough. connections: 𝗕𝗮𝘀𝗮𝗹 𝘃𝗲𝗶𝗻 𝗼𝗳 𝗥𝗼𝘀𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗵𝗮𝗹 (𝗕𝗩𝗥) 𝗗𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗣𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗻𝘀: BVR drainage is classified into three main types based on their anatomical course and termination: 𝗧𝘆𝗽𝗲 𝗔 (𝗡𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝗹 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗻𝘂𝗼𝘂𝘀): The BVR is a continuous vessel that drains primarily posteriorly into the vein of Galen. 𝗧𝘆𝗽𝗲 𝗕 (𝗡𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝗹 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗻𝘂𝗼𝘂𝘀): This pattern features dual drainage. The BVR drains both anteriorly into the cavernous sinus (via the uncal vein) and posteriorly into the vein of Galen. 𝗧𝘆𝗽𝗲 𝗖 (𝗣𝗿𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲): This is considered an abnormal variant where the BVR drains directly into dural sinuses—such as the cavernous, superior petrosal, or tentorial sinuses—rather than the Galenic system. In this pattern, the middle and posterior segments of the BVR are often absent. 𝗔𝘀𝘀𝗼𝗰𝗶𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗡𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗻𝗲𝘂𝗿𝘆𝘀𝗺𝗮𝗹 𝗣𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗺𝗲𝘀𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗽𝗵𝗮𝗹𝗶𝗰 𝗛𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗿𝗵𝗮𝗴𝗲 (𝗡𝗔𝗣𝗛): A meta-analysis of 888 patients reveals that primitive (Type C) drainage is a potential risk factor and diagnostic indicator for NAPH. Key findings include: 𝗣𝗿𝗲𝘃𝗮𝗹𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲: Patients with NAPH are significantly more likely to have a primitive BVR pattern in at least one hemisphere compared to those with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH) (47.7% vs. 22.1%). 𝗜𝗻𝗱𝗶𝘃𝗶𝗱𝘂𝗮𝗹 𝗩𝗲𝗻𝗼𝘂𝘀 𝗦𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺𝘀: When individual systems are analyzed, NAPH patients show a much higher rate of primitive venous drainage than aSAH patients (34.9% vs. 15.3%). NAPH patients are far less likely to have bilateral normal (Type A) drainage systems (18.3%) compared to aSAH patients (37.4%). 𝗖𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝘅𝘁 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗠𝗲𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗶𝘀𝗺𝘀: Direct connection of perimesencephalic veins to dural sinuses in the primitive pattern may predispose these veins to rupture during sudden increases in venous pressure, such as during a Valsalva maneuver or straining. Furthermore, some primitive veins cross the tentorial margin, making them susceptible to torsion or friction. While NAPH remains a diagnosis of exclusion, the identification of a primitive BVR drainage pattern on imaging can help clinicians affirm the diagnosis of NAPH and support a venous origin for the hemorrhage. connections: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei says AI development needs to slow down before the risks become too hard to control. “We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models.” Amodei says the main problem is speed. AI models are improving faster than safety work can keep up, while the systems themselves are becoming far more capable. He warned that within 6 to 12 months, AI could become powerful enough to run large groups of agents that cause major cyber damage, including attacks on key parts of the internet. Another concern is AI helping build better AI. If models start speeding up the work needed to create the next generation of models, progress could move much faster than humans can track. Amodei says even slowing development by one or two years could give researchers far more time to work out how to keep these systems safe. about: I am a neuroscientist and associate professor at the Université de Montréal and principal investigator of the Murphy-Royal Lab, where we explore how brain cells called astrocytes shape neural function, behaviour, and the response to stress. Our research bridges synaptic physiology, cellular metabolism, and behavioural neuroscience to uncover how stress alters astrocyte structure and function — and how those changes influence neural circuits and behaviour. Using cutting-edge techniques including in vivo imaging, electrophysiology, and behavioural assays in animal models, my team investigates mechanisms underlying stress-related disorders such as anxiety, depression and PTSD. We are particularly focused on astrocyte-neuron interactions, astrocytic support of synaptic metabolism, and metabolic regulation of plasticity and behaviour. My work has been published in leading journals, and has advanced understanding of how glial cells actively shape brain function and behavioural outcomes. I am driven by questions at the intersection of stress biology, synaptic physiology, and systems neuroscience — and I thrive in collaborative, interdisciplinary environments that push the boundaries of how we think about brain-behavior relationships.

connections: An estimated 6.7 million people in the U.S. over the age of 65 are living with Alzheimer's disease. The progressive disease destroys brain cells resulting in a gradual decline in a person’s ability to remember, pay attention, reason, and this gets worse overtime. #NIH_IRP researchers are exploring a protein in neurons called DPP6 and its connection to #Alzheimer 's disease. Researchers found that old mice that did not have DPP6, share many characteristics with Alzheimer's disease. By studying the #hippocampus , a part of the brain that plays a major role in learning and memory, they uncovered some structures that appear as clusters of abnormal, swollen (sick) presynaptic terminals, a part of the nervous system that plays a crucial role in transmitting signals between neurons. This image from the lab of Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD) ’s Dr. Dax Hoffman shows that the discovery of a novel NeuN+ structure (green) is abnormal. It shows nuclei (blue) and enlarged presynaptic swellings, resulting from synapse loss and neuronal death impacted by DPP6. Synapse loss is tied to sensory, motor, and cognitive impairments.

connections: Environmental Neurotoxins Awareness: Safeguarding #Brain #Health in a Toxic World Modern neuroscience increasingly acknowledges the profound effects of environmental exposures on cognitive health, emotional regulation, neurodevelopment, and neurodegeneration. The brain, with its high lipid content, rich vascularization, and energy demands, is acutely vulnerable to environmental insults—particularly neurotoxicants that are now widespread in consumer products, food systems, and digital infrastructure. Neurotoxins disrupt central nervous system function via multiple mechanisms: oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, neuroinflammation, excitotoxicity, and endocrine disruption. In this context, a neuroscience-informed lifestyle must prioritize not only cognitive stimulation and nutrition, but also exposure reduction and detoxification support. Below, I outline the primary environmental neurotoxins of concern and evidence-based strategies to mitigate their effects. 1. Electromagnetic Fields (EMF): A Subtle but Ubiquitous Stressor Electromagnetic fields—emanating from Wi-Fi routers, smartphones, laptops, and power lines—are a form of non-ionizing radiation. Though less potent than ionizing radiation (e.g., X-rays), chronic EMF exposure is increasingly studied for its potential role in neurophysiological dysregulation. Human Data: Epidemiological evidence remains mixed, but early-life EMF exposure has been correlated with behavioral dysregulation and increased oxidative markers in some pediatric populations. Neuroscientific Guidance: Limit EMF proximity during sleep (remove phone from bedside, use airplane mode). Use hardwired Ethernet connections for computers when possible. Turn off Wi-Fi at night to support circadian brain detox (glymphatic clearance). 2. Plastics & BPA: Endocrine Disruptors That Interfere with Brain Development Bisphenol A (BPA) and its analogs—widely found in plastic containers, receipts, and food linings—are potent xenoestrogens. They disrupt the endocrine system, which intricately interacts with the central nervous system across development and adult cognition. Neurodevelopmental Risk: Prenatal BPA exposure is associated with impaired executive function, reduced working memory, and increased anxiety in children. BPA interferes with estrogen receptor signaling in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex—regions central to learning and behavioral regulation. Neuroimmune Link: BPA elevates microglial activation and increases pro-inflammatory cytokines in the brain, exacerbating vulnerability to mood disorders and neurodegeneration. Mitigation Strategies: Use glass, stainless steel, or certified BPA/BPS-free containers. Avoid microwaving plastic or storing acidic foods in plastic. Choose fresh, unpackaged foods when possible to reduce cumulative plastic ingestion. … more

about: I lead the Research to Understand Stroke due to Haemorrhage (RUSH) programme, which is dedicated to improving the outcome for adults who have diseases that may cause, or have caused, intracranial hemorrhage. The fundamental study designs of clinical epidemiology - such as randomised controlled trials, community- or population-based cohort and case-control studies, brain banking, and meta-analysis - are the foundation of my focus on the frequency, prognosis, treatment, and pathophysiology of intracranial haemorrhage. I also care for people with these conditions, audit their care, and help undergraduate and postgraduate students to develop and answer research questions within the RUSH programme. I became interested in neurology during undergraduate medical training at Cambridge University. I was inspired to work on common neurological problems by Charles Warlow and the stroke research group in Edinburgh, which I joined in 1998 as an MRC clinical training fellow, progressing to MRC patient-oriented clinician scientist and senior clinical fellowships until 2016. Since becoming a professor of clinical neurology at the University of Edinburgh in August 2013, the depth and breadth of my research has expanded beyond stroke and intracranial haemorrhage in response to several of the global challenges in non-communicable diseases, vascular multi-morbidity, cerebral small vessel diseases, and therapeutic dilemmas provoked by vascular ageing. My lived experience of clinical research has made me concerned about increasing the value of biomedical research by minimising waste in the choice of research question, study design, study conduct, regulation, and reporting. This led to me becoming one of the lead authors of The Lancet's 2014 Series on Increasing Value and Reducing Waste in Research (www.thelancet.com/series/research) and the related campaign (www.thelancet.com/campaigns/efficiency), as well as a founding member of the REWARD Alliance (http://rewardalliance.net).

connections: For persons exposed to particularly intense or prolonged stress growing up, the functional communication between prefrontal and the amygdala *stays* disrupted, even into adulthood. For them it is not a matter of doing something to activate prefrontal (like naming what they are feeling). Even when they recruit prefrontal cortex, amygdala activity is not correspondingly reduced because the message from prefrontal is not getting through. Many people who have experienced severe early life stress stay in an anxious, hyper-vigilant state as adults, constantly on the alert for possible danger, easily and overly panicked, immobilized by things that provoke anxiety. But the extremely encouraging news is that the anatomical connection between prefrontal cortex and the amygdala is still there. It never went away. I have hypothesized that when therapy, or an intervention, succeeds in helping someone recover from complex developmental trauma or PTSD, the neural mechanism underlying that recovery is that the communication between prefrontal and the amygdala has been restored; the brain’s mechanism for calming down the amygdala is working again. … more

Yael also writes fiction, including the cinematic script for Activision’s best selling video game, “True Crime: Streets of LA”.
